title: A Disease Once Nearly Forgotten
shared_passage:
Listen to a short excerpt from a popular radio program called 1A and answer the questions.

PRESENTER: America's first polio case in nearly a decade was discovered in Rockland county, New York, this spring. There are now believed to be hundreds of cases in the area. Polio was one of the most feared diseases in the US in the early 1950s. It caused more than 15,000 cases of paralysis in a year. That all changed in 1955.

PUBLIC SERVICE ANNOUNCER: Today, the tragedy of paralytic polio can be prevented in individuals protected by all three recommended doses of polio vaccine. However, there are still millions of Americans who have received only one or two of the doses, or none at all. These are today's potential victims. You can avoid all the expense, suffering, and heartache that paralytic polio causes if you make use of the vaccine that is now available.

PRESENTER: That was a public service announcement from the 1950s urging Americans to get the new polio vaccine. My dad was born in 1938 before the vaccine was available. And he contracted polio as a young child. The disease left him with a severe limp, and he suffered from related muscle weakness later in life. I saw the effects of polio on my dad's life. And some of you shared your own memories of how the disease shaped your lives.

WOMAN: My parents cried when the polio vaccine came out. We were eight children, and very vulnerable. We were not allowed to swim in municipal swimming pools in the summer. My family, we collected dimes for the March of Dimes Polio Research. My best friend's mother had polio, and she needed crutches all her life.

PRESENTER: For 40 years, the US has been polio-free. How do we make sure polio doesn't return to the US? And what should you be doing to protect yourself and your loved ones? Joining us now is Dr. Jose R. Romero. He's the director of the CDC's National Center for Immunization and Respiratory Diseases. Dr. Romero, welcome to the program.

DR. ROMERO: Thank you, Ms White. Thank you very much. And thank you for sharing that personal anecdote with us.

PRESENTER: Of course. Now, this case in Rockland county, New York, was the first documented polio case in the US, as I said, in nearly a decade. Why are we seeing new cases appear now?

DR. ROMERO: It has to do with the fact that immunization rates are lower in some communities than others. And so, with an incursion of poliovirus that can cause paralysis, those populations are extremely vulnerable. This is a disease, as you've mentioned before, that can be prevented by a vaccine that we have experience with for over 50 years. It's safe and effective. So people can take control of this and prevent this disease by taking the vaccine.

PRESENTER: Now, the man who contracted the virus was unvaccinated against polio. Here's a clip of chief medical advisor, Dr. Anthony Fauci, speaking to NPR yesterday about vaccination rates in the county where the outbreak started.

DR. FAUCI: Polio is 99% preventable by vaccines. If you look at certain places in New York, such as in Rockland County, only about 60% of the children are vaccinated, and in some sections of the county, as few as 37% are vaccinated. That's unacceptable. You've got to get the children vaccinated.

PRESENTER: How do these rates square up with the rest of the country?

DR. ROMERO: So, they're much lower. So, overall, the United States, we're about 94 to 95% vaccinated. And even in New York state, 93, 94% of the population has antibodies for polio from vaccination.
